Anything that takes longer than a request should not happen inside the request. This module covers the four ways to run work in the background in Rust, from a spawned task to a durable queue.

The four options

Approach Durability Complexity Use when
tokio::spawn none — lost on restart trivial fire-and-forget, e.g. cache warm
In-process channel + worker none low burst smoothing, low value
Postgres table + SKIP LOCKED full low you already have Postgres
Redis / SQS / RabbitMQ full medium high volume, cross-language

Rule of thumb: start with tokio::spawn. Move to a Postgres queue the day losing a job would cost money. Do not add Redis on day one.

Option 1: tokio::spawn

Two things to be careful about:

  • A panicking task is silent. The JoinHandle is dropped, so nothing observes the panic. Log inside the task.
  • An aborted process loses the work. If the pod restarts mid-email, the email never happens.

For a small number of known-at-startup tasks, keep the handles and supervise them:

Option 2: bounded channel + worker pool

A bounded channel gives you backpressure: when workers are saturated, submit awaits instead of growing memory without limit. That is the whole point of mpsc::channel(1000) rather than unbounded_channel().

Option 3: a Postgres-backed queue (the workhorse)

One table, one index, FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED. No extra infrastructure.

Enqueue

Because it is a normal table, enqueuing can happen inside the same transaction as the business write. That is the killer feature: the job and the row it refers to commit or roll back together. No dual-write problem.

Claim

FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED means N workers never claim the same row and never block each other. This is the entire trick.

Complete / fail

The worker loop

Reclaiming stuck jobs

A worker that dies mid-job leaves a row in running forever. Add a reaper:

Run it from the same worker loop every 60 s with stale_after_secs = 300. Without this, one crashed pod silently stops processing a subset of your jobs.

Gotcha: the reaper can resurrect a job that is genuinely still running (a long task, not a dead worker). Either set stale_after above your longest job, or have handlers be idempotent. Idempotency is the real answer.

Idempotency

Every handler should tolerate running twice:

A unique constraint plus ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING gives you exactly-once semantics on top of at-least-once delivery. This pattern works for emails, webhooks, invoices and payments.

Scheduling: cron in Rust

For a single-replica scheduler this is fine. With multiple replicas, every pod runs it — use a Postgres advisory lock to elect one:

Alert on jobs_pending growing monotonically for 10 minutes — that is the signature of a stuck consumer, and it is invisible without a metric.

Exercises

  1. Implement the Postgres queue: schema, enqueue, claim, complete, fail.
  2. Run three worker processes concurrently and prove no job is processed twice (count rows in a processed table).
  3. Add exponential backoff and verify run_at increases on repeated failures.
  4. Write the reaper and test it by inserting a running job with an old locked_at.
  5. Make the welcome-email handler idempotent with a unique constraint.
  6. Add a /admin/jobs endpoint returning counts by status.
